summary: Aims to focus discussion on problems of policy requirements for routing between administrative domains. It does not propose standards. It hopes general agreement emerges toward a solution.

eli5.summary: Different owners of networks have different rules for traffic. This lists what those rules need so people can work out a fair way to follow them.

questions: policy requirements for inter administrative domain routing
what policies do routing domains need
what are access and charging policies
subtitle: A 1989 list of what independently run networks will want to control when routing traffic between each other.

tldr.problem: The Research Internet had grown into a tangle of backbones, regional networks, campuses and private networks, each owned by a different organization with its own rules about who may use its resources and at what cost.
tldr.mechanism: The memo argues that routing must take those rules into account. It sets out assumptions about how the networks are connected, then classifies the policies that Administrative Domains will want to enforce, with example statements from federal agencies.
tldr.outcome: It proposes no standard. It is meant as input for the functional specification and evaluation of a new policy routing protocol, and it points to RFC 1102 as the approach that best fits the requirements.

facts.label: Policy Term fields
facts.value: Source, destination, UCI, global and bilateral conditions

today: RFC 1125 is a 1989 discussion memo that proposed no standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It refers to RFC 1102 as the policy routing approach that matches its requirements.

sections.title: Background and the Policy Routing Problem
sections.content:
RFC 1125 is a discussion memo. Its status section says that no proposed solutions in it are intended as standards, and that the hope is for general consensus to emerge, leading eventually to standards.

The Research Internet had evolved from a single backbone with many connected campus networks into several cross-country backbones, regional access networks and many campus networks. Unlike the telephone network, which has lateral connections only at the highest level, the Research Internet has lateral connections at every level of the hierarchy. Private companies add more complexity, including private wide area networks that overlap with backbone or regional networks.

Organizational boundaries in this topology define Administrative Domains (ADs): sets of hosts and network resources governed by common policies. Because of these boundaries, no single, centralized set of policies can be imposed on all resources. Policy Routing (PR) is the routing needed to choose inter-AD routes by policy-related parameters such as cost and access rights, in addition to connectivity and congestion.

The memo also separates two kinds of AD. A stub AD is mainly concerned with traffic to and from its own hosts. A transit AD is mainly concerned with carrying packets to and from other ADs. Controlling transit alone would not let an AD control the path of its own packets or implement flexible charging.
sections.eli5: Many different owners run pieces of the network, like different towns owning different roads. Each town has its own rules, so a trip has to follow every town's rules along the way.

sections.title: Why the Problem Is Difficult
sections.content:
The memo names four constraints that limit the solution space.

  • No global authority. Each AD sets policy for its own traffic and resources. Complete autonomy would mean no communication, so mechanisms should let ADs design their boundaries instead of making them impenetrable or removing them.
  • Resource sharing as well as interconnection. Sharing links and gateways, or providing transit, is harder to control than plain interconnection. A packet may cross several transit ADs, so all of their policies must be considered, which means enforcement has to be built into the routing protocols and cannot be left to the end points.
  • Users do not map neatly to ADs. Legitimate users of one agency's resources may sit inside a campus AD, and users can move. PR must therefore identify principals and associate rights with them, not only identify resources.
  • Accountability across ADs. This can be enforced before use (access control) or after the fact (record keeping or metering). The memo argues that resource usage should be visible to users across AD boundaries, whether or not anyone is actually charged.
sections.eli5: Nobody is in charge of everyone. Many owners share roads, people belong to more than one group, and everyone wants to know who used what.

sections.title: Two Models of Internet Topology
sections.content:
The memo says most of the community expected the future Internet to connect on the order of 150,000,000 termination points and 100,000 ADs, but opinions differed about the shape of the topology.

The simple model says the complex topology is a passing artifact. Public carriers will provide pervasive, competitively priced, high speed data services, the ADs will form a clean hierarchy with no lateral connections or bypass links, and policy will reduce to charging. Routing could then be a least cost path with the metric in dollars and cents, and the routing protocol would not need to change much.

The complex model, which the memo supports, assumes a mostly hierarchical structure with persistent exceptions: roughly 100 long haul transit ADs, tens of thousands of regional ADs and hundreds of thousands of stub ADs. Stub ADs will keep private lateral links for political, technical and reliability reasons, and many companies will keep private long haul networks. ADs will then want controls that cannot be captured in a single cost metric, so lateral connections must be supported along with ways to control their use in the routing protocols.

The memo allows that some ADs may form a federation and negotiate away their differences, but it expects collections of ADs that will not and cannot behave as one federation.
sections.eli5: One group thinks the future is a tidy tree where only price matters. The author thinks it will stay messy, with side roads and private roads, so people need more kinds of rules.

sections.title: A Taxonomy of Policies
sections.content:
The memo splits policies into two classes. Access policies say who can use resources and under what conditions, usually in the form: principals of type x can have access to resources of type y under conditions z. Charging policies specify metering, accounting and billing.

Access policies may specify these parameters:

  • Source/destination: restrict communication from or to particular ADs, hosts or user classes.
  • Path: allow or refuse passing through particular ADs en route. The most general form depends on any AD in the path; a more modest form looks only at neighboring ADs.
  • Quality or type of service: restrict special resources, such as a high throughput, low delay link.
  • Resource guarantee: guarantee a share of a resource that others may use when it is idle.
  • Temporal: restrict by time of day or similar.
  • High level protocol: restrict to something like mail or file transfer.
  • Resource limit: cap traffic over a time interval.
  • Authentication requirements: demand cryptographic proof of identity.

Charging policies may specify the unit of accounting, the basis for charging (for example per Kbyte or per Kpkt), the actual charges, who is charged or paid, whose packet count is used, and a bound on charges. Policy types usually appear in combination.
sections.eli5: Rules can be about who you are, where you came from, which road you take, how fast you go, what time it is, or how much you pay. Most owners mix several kinds.

sections.title: Policy Terms and Agency Examples
sections.content:
The memo writes example policies in a Policy Term (PT) notation suggested by Dave Clark in RFC 1102. A PT has the form [(Hsrc,ADsrc,ADent),(Hdst,ADdst,ADexit),UCI,Cg,Cb]: source host, source AD and entering AD, then destination host, destination AD and exit AD, followed by a user class identifier (UCI), global conditions and bilateral conditions. A null entry for the exit AD marks a transit restriction; naming the AD itself as source or destination marks a source/destination policy.

The examples were collected in the fall of 1988 through interviews with representatives of federal agencies. The RFC stresses that they are not official policy. They cover NSF, DOE, NASA, DARPA and DCA, and for example NASA would accept traffic to or from its own members but allow no transit, and DCA would carry no transit traffic and charge for all packets by the kilopacket. The memo also gives two hypothetical regional networks, and says that interviews with regionals, campuses, private networks and commercial carriers were not yet complete or possible.
sections.eli5: To show what the rules look like, the author wrote down what real agencies said they wanted, in a short fill-in-the-blanks form. They are only examples, not official rules.

sections.title: Problem Requirements and Existing Mechanisms
sections.content:
The memo flags three requirements as problematic from a technical feasibility view. Non-interference policies, which grant access only while the AD's own use is not hurt, depend on a highly dynamic local value that is not globally available, and could cause looping, oscillation and excessive route recomputation. Very fine granularity may be better handled by network level or end system access controls. Security is expensive: routing protocols are open to impersonation, data substitution and denial of service, and preventing misuse in advance costs cryptographic overhead per connection or per packet.

Looking at mechanisms, the memo says EGP, DGP and BGP carry a notion of policy about where routing database information travels but are not meant for policy based routing of packets. Landmark and Cartesian could restrict forwarding but do not suit some of the policy types. Of the three classes of mechanism described in RFC 1104, only policy based packet forwarding, as in RFC 1102, is expressive enough, and it also lets stub ADs control routes through source routing.
sections.eli5: Some wishes are hard to grant, like "you can use my road unless I am busy," because busy changes every second. The author thinks one existing design could handle most of the rest.

items.title: Source/destination
items.text: Restrict traffic from or to particular ADs, hosts or user classes.

items.title: Path
items.text: Allow or refuse particular ADs along the route.

items.title: Quality of service
items.text: Limit access to special high throughput or low delay resources.

items.title: Resource guarantee
items.text: Guarantee a share of a resource to a chosen party.

items.title: Temporal
items.text: Limit use by time of day.

items.title: High level protocol
items.text: Allow only protocols such as mail or file transfer.

items.title: Resource limit
items.text: Cap traffic over a time interval.
